title: What If an Astronaut Let Go of the Ship? In 1984 One Did, on Purpose

scenes.text: What if an astronaut let go of the spaceship, no rope? In 1984 one did, on purpose.
February 7th, 1984. Bruce McCandless stepped out of the shuttle Challenger wearing a jet backpack and no tether.
scenes.keywords: space shuttle open cargo bay orbit

scenes.text: Two dozen nitrogen jets, controlled by hand. He drifted away at less than a foot per second to save gas.
He stopped 320 feet out: a human satellite, 170 miles above the Atlantic, moving at 23 times the speed of sound.
scenes.keywords: astronaut small against earth from space

scenes.text: Behind him a crewmate waited at the robot arm to grab him if the jets failed.
Nearly six hours later he was back inside. His joke: a small step for Neil, a heck of a big leap for me. The photo became one of the most famous ever taken.

description:
What if an astronaut let go of the ship? On 7 February 1984 Bruce McCandless flew the nitrogen-powered Manned Maneuvering Unit untethered to about 320 feet from the shuttle Challenger, 170 miles above Earth, the first free-flying spacewalk.
He moved at under a foot per second to conserve gas, a crewmate stood ready at the robot arm to grab him, and pilot Robert Gibson took the now-famous photograph through the cabin window. The spacewalk lasted almost six hours.
What should we run through next?
thumbnail_text: WHAT IF YOU LET GO IN SPACE?
first_comment: McCandless helped design the jet backpack himself, and he had been the voice of mission control talking to Neil Armstrong during the Moon landing. Would you let go? And what should we run through next?
